title: Dockerfile Masterclass
subtitle: From first instruction to production-grade image
description: Learn to write Dockerfiles that are small, reproducible, secure and fast to rebuild. This is the highest-leverage skill in everyday Docker work.
outcomes: Choose the right instruction for each layer
Use multi-stage builds to ship only runtime artifacts
Order layers and .dockerignore for effective caching
Harden images with non-root users and read-only patterns

modules.title: Instructions and semantics
modules.summary: The grammar of a Dockerfile and the instructions that matter.

lessons.title: Dockerfile anatomy
lessons.summary: Every instruction is a decision about layers, build context, or runtime defaults.
objectives: Explain COPY vs ADD and RUN vs CMD

sections.title: A recipe, executed top to bottom
sections.body:
A Dockerfile is a sequence of instructions executed by the builder. Filesystem-changing instructions (`RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD`) create layers. Metadata instructions (`ENV`, `EXPOSE`, `LABEL`, `WORKDIR`, `USER`) update the image config. `FROM` starts a new build stage.

Only files in the **build context** can be copied. The context is sent to the builder, so a large context slows every build even if the file is not copied.

sections.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:20-alpine

WORKDIR /app

# Dependencies first: this layer is cached until the lockfile changes
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

# Application code second
COPY . .

ENV NODE_ENV=production
EXPOSE 3000
USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
sections.note: The `# syntax` directive pins the Dockerfile frontend, enabling modern features consistently across engines.

sections.title: Prefer COPY over ADD
sections.body: ADD has extra behaviours (URLs, auto-extraction) that are surprising and bypass .dockerignore expectations. Use COPY unless you specifically need ADD.

questions.question: Which instructions create filesystem layers?
questions.explain: Only instructions that change the filesystem produce layers.

questions.question: Why is build context size important?
options: The whole context is sent to the builder
questions.explain: A large context is transferred even if unused.

questions.question: What does WORKDIR do?
options: Sets the working directory for following instructions and runtime

lessons.title: ENTRYPOINT vs CMD
lessons.summary: The two runtime instructions, exec form vs shell form, and how arguments flow.
objectives: Predict what runs for every combination of ENTRYPOINT and CMD
Use exec form for correct signal handling

sections.title: Defaults versus the executable
sections.body:
`ENTRYPOINT` sets the executable. `CMD` sets default arguments (or the whole command if there is no ENTRYPOINT). `docker run image arg` replaces CMD but keeps ENTRYPOINT. That is the contract that makes images configurable without a rebuild.

Use **exec form** (`["node","server.js"]`) so the process is PID 1 and receives signals directly. Shell form (`node server.js`) wraps the command in `/bin/sh -c`; the shell becomes PID 1 and may not forward SIGTERM.

head: ENTRYPOINT
CMD
Result
rows: docker run img worker.js → node worker.js

sections.code:
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
# Exec form: node is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM
ENTRYPOINT ["node"]
CMD ["server.js"]
sections.note: Now `docker run IMAGE worker.js` runs the worker without changing the image.

sections.title: Do not use shell form for services
sections.body: Shell form hides signal handling behind /bin/sh. If you need shell features at startup, use an entrypoint script that ends with `exec "$@"`.

questions.question: What happens to CMD when you pass arguments to docker run?
questions.explain: Runtime arguments replace CMD, not ENTRYPOINT.

questions.question: Which form gives PID 1 signal handling?
questions.explain: Exec form runs the binary directly.

lessons.title: Multi-stage builds
lessons.summary: Build with a full toolchain, ship only the artifact. The single biggest image-size win.

sections.title: Stages are named build environments
sections.body:
Each `FROM ... AS name` starts a stage. Only the final stage becomes the image. Files can be copied from earlier stages with `COPY --from=name`. Build tools, caches, source and test dependencies stay behind.

This works for compiled languages, but also for Node: install dev dependencies and build, then copy `dist` and production `node_modules` into a slim runtime stage.

sections.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:20-alpine AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci

FROM deps AS build
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev

FROM node:20-alpine AS runtime
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY package.json ./
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
sections.note: The runtime stage contains no source, dev dependencies, or build cache.

sections.code:
# Build only a specific stage for debugging
docker build --target build -t app:debug .

# Compare sizes
docker image ls app

sections.title: Use --target in development
sections.body: A `dev` stage can include hot reload and test tools while CI builds the minimal runtime stage. One Dockerfile, different targets.

lessons.title: Layer caching and .dockerignore
lessons.summary: Why the same Dockerfile rebuilds in two seconds for one person and two minutes for another.

sections.title: Cache keys
sections.body:
The builder caches each layer keyed by the parent layer, the instruction, and the input files. If the parent or input changes, that layer and every later layer miss. This is why dependency manifests are copied before source code: source changes should not invalidate dependency installation.

For `COPY`, the cache key includes file metadata and content. A changed lockfile correctly invalidates `npm ci`. A changed README should not invalidate it if the README is excluded or copied later.

sections.code:
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
sections.note: BuildKit cache mounts keep the package manager cache between builds without baking it into a layer.
Excluding node_modules is critical: the host copy can shadow the container install and is often platform-specific.

sections.title: A cache hit is not always correct
sections.body: If a build depends on a remote URL or unpinned package version, the cache may hide an update. Use `--no-cache` for deliberate refreshes and pin versions for reproducibility.

lessons.title: Production Dockerfile patterns
lessons.summary: Non-root, pinned bases, health checks, labels and a build that fails closed.
objectives: Harden the runtime user and filesystem
Pin and document the base image
Add health checks and OCI labels

sections.title: Production checklist
sections.body: A production image should run as a non-root user, use a minimal pinned base, avoid build tools, handle signals, expose only what is needed, and carry provenance labels. Add a health check so orchestrators can distinguish "process alive" from "service ready".

sections.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7
FROM node:20.18-alpine3.20 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev

FROM node:20.18-alpine3.20
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.title="acme/api" \
      org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/acme/api" \
      org.opencontainers.image.version="1.4.0"
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/dist ./dist
COPY --chown=node:node package.json ./
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=10s --retries=3 \
  CMD node -e "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:3000/health').then(r=>process.exit(r.ok?0:1)).catch(()=>process.exit(1))"
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
sections.note: Use distroless or scratch equivalents where possible. Alpine is shown for familiarity, not as a universal best choice.

Pattern
rows: Read-only root + tmpfs for writable paths

Keep them in a builder stage only

sections.title: Never bake secrets into layers
sections.body: Anything in a layer can be extracted even if deleted in a later layer. BuildKit `--mount=type=secret` keeps secrets out of history.

questions.question: Which user should a production process run as?
questions.explain: Non-root limits the blast radius of a compromise.

questions.question: How do you use a secret during build without persisting it?

questions.question: What does a HEALTHCHECK enable?
